activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The roast chicken was half eaten and Stella's grandmother was already crying, quietly, into her napkin, when Alexane texted a photo from the parking lot of the restaurant asking if she could come in. Stella excused herself from the table and stood by the hostess stand in her graduation dress, which was starting to itch.

"You said family only," Piper had warned her that afternoon, pinning the tassel back onto Stella's cap. "Your grandmother counts the chairs."

But Alexane had driven forty minutes because Stella had left the ceremony early, before the mortarboards went up, and everyone knew why even though nobody had said it. Stella's father had been in the hospital in March and April and most of May, and the family had adjudicated his attendance like a panel of judges, weighing oxygen tanks against wheelchair ramps against the May heat, and in the end he had watched the livestream from his recliner while everyone else sat in the bleachers. He was at the dinner now, pale, folded into the corner chair, and that was supposed to be the whole victory.

Alexane came in carrying a bakery box. "You left before they threw the caps," she said, hugging Stella hard enough to wrinkle the dress. "So I stole one."

The box held a single black cap, slightly dented, Piper's name still inked inside the band. The whole table turned, and Stella's mother made room and Alexane got squeezed in between two cousins, and for a while the dinner was loud again, Piper's mother Facetiming from the restaurant across town so Piper could wave at Stella, her aunts shouting congratulations into the phone.

Stella was quieter than the table deserved. She kept looking at her father's plate, at how he moved the food around with the patience of a man conserving strength, and she kept thinking that this was the last dinner that would ever be arranged around all of them in this configuration, the last time her grandmother would cry over her in a restaurant in their town. Everyone kept saying congratulations and it sounded like a door closing. When her uncle proposed a toast to the graduate, she raised her glass and felt the sadness arrive in a somatic wave, her throat tight, her hands cold around the stem, the body announcing what the mouth wouldn't.

Alexane leaned across the cousins. "You're doing the face."

"What face."

"The one from the debate tournament, when you lose on a technicality and pretend you're fine." Alexane took a roll from the basket, buttered it with unnecessary care. "You keep saying goodbye to everything like it's already gone."

"It is gone. That's what graduation is."

"It's called commencement," Alexane said. "The word means beginning."

Stella blinked at her. "It does not."

"It does. That's why they used it for the ceremonies, because graduates begin a new status. Like becoming a bachelor, or a master. Look it up." She held out her phone, screen already lit, and Stella read the entry twice under the table while her uncles argued about parking. She had walked across a stage that morning under a word she had never once thought about, a word that had been standing in the program the whole time, patiently insisting on itself.

She didn't feel converted, exactly. The grief was still real; the town and the schedule and the eleven friends she'd eaten lunch with every day since sophomore year were genuinely ending, and no etymology could adjudicate that away, and she didn't want it to. But she could hold both, she thought, turning the phone off. She could be sad about the closing door and curious about the hallway behind it, and the two didn't cancel out; they sat in her chest together, uncomfortably, like two relatives at the same wedding. College was in September, four hours north, and she had been dreading it and craving it in equal measure since the acceptance letter, and now she understood that the ceremony she'd fled had actually been named for the craving.

Her father caught her eye across the table. He looked tired but present, upright in his chair, and he lifted his water glass an inch, a private toast meant for no one else.

"Come outside with me for a second," Stella said to Alexane and Piper's pixelated face on the phone. In the parking lot the evening had cooled, and the asphalt still held the day's heat through her thin shoes. She took the stolen cap out of the box, set it on her head, and pulled the tassel across from right to left, the way they'd been taught. Piper, on the screen, whooped.

"Throw it," Alexane said.

Stella looked up at the sky, at the first pale stars over the strip mall, at her family visible through the restaurant window laughing at something her uncle had said, and she thought about keeping the cap somewhere safe, boxed, finished. Then she threw it. It went higher than she expected, wobbling against the dark, and Alexane caught it on the second bounce off a parked sedan.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
John had been at his grandfather's house for two days, and the essay was due in five, and all he had was John Lewis Gaddis and a feeling that one historian was not enough. His grandfather's study smelled of pipe tobacco he was no longer allowed to smoke and held a wall of books nobody had opened since roughly the fall of the Berlin Wall, which John thought was fitting, since the fall of the Berlin Wall was more or less his topic.

"You look like a boy being digested," his grandfather said from the doorway, holding two mugs of tea.

"I need a second historian. If I only use Gaddis I'm basically writing his book report with extra steps."

"Then find one who disagrees with him." His grandfather set a mug down on a coaster shaped like a trout. "Disagreement is how the discipline stays honest."

John texted Brandon, who had already finished his essay and would not stop mentioning it. The reply came fast: "check leffler. melvyn leffler, A Preponderance of Power. it won the 1993 bancroft prize. it argued us leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world. you owe me a milkshake." Then a second message: "chocolate. large. i keep receipts."

John found the book at the public library the next morning, checked out under his grandfather's card because John had left his at home, which his grandfather found hilarious. He carried it back through the July heat and spread it on the kitchen table beside Gaddis, a historian on either side of the salt shaker, facing each other like duelists. Maina came over in the afternoon because her family was visiting relatives three doors down and she claimed exile.

"So one says the Soviets started it," she said, flipping a fork between her fingers, "and the other says?"

"The other says look at what America actually did, not what it said. Leffler's whole thing is preponderance. Power piled up until nobody could touch us."

"That sounds like a biome," Maina said. "One big dominant species and everything else adapting around it."

"That is a much better metaphor than anything in my draft," John said, and wrote it on his hand.

His grandfather interposed himself at the counter, pouring more tea, pretending not to listen in the way of grandfathers everywhere. "You know what Bancroft Prize means?" he asked.

"Brandon says it's a big deal."

"It is a big deal. It means his peers thought the argument was worth taking seriously, even the ones who hated it."

John spent the evening in the study with the lamp on, doing what Mr. Rao had told their class to do in the spring: test the explanation against the evidence. If Gaddis was right about Soviet expansionism driving everything, then American moves should look reactive, hesitant, dragged into commitments. He read the Marshall Plan documents twice. They did not look hesitant. They looked like men who had decided the shape of the postwar world before the war had quite finished, and who were building it the way you build a fence, generously, around everyone else.

But when he tried to write Leffler down as the winner, his pen stopped. Dominance explained the Marshall Plan and NATO and the bases. It explained less, he thought, why the Americans kept missing what the Soviets were actually doing, why the fear kept outrunning the facts. He wrote a paragraph arguing Leffler, crossed out the last sentence, and wrote in the margin, honest but unproven, which he suspected was not the kind of margin note that got full marks.

At dinner his grandfather asked how the duel was going. "You've reached the part where nobody wins," he said, ladling soup.

"That's the worst part," John said. "The assignment says compare and evaluate, and I want there to be an answer."

"There is an answer. The answer is you read the evidence and it fits Leffler better on some days and Gaddis better on others, and you say so. That's not a failure, that's the job." He pointed his spoon at John. "Also you owe Brandon a milkshake, and I'd like to be driven there when you go, since he chose a good book."

Maina, who had stayed for soup, reached over and tapped the back of John's hand. "Your note's sweating off. What's it say?"

John turned his hand over. BIOME, it read, smudged but legible.

"That," he said, "is my second paragraph."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Chinese New Year's Eve reunion dinner, fish is traditionally served because the word for fish, 'yu', sounds like the word for surplus or abundance.
story:
The fish arrived still cold from the market, wrapped in newspaper that smelled of ink and riverwater, and Carson's grandmother set it on the counter with the authority of someone depositing a diplomatic pouch. "Whole fish," she said. "Head on. Tail on. Do not argue with me about this."

"I wasn't going to argue," Carson said, though he had been composing an argument in his head for two blocks, something about how fillets were easier to steam and nobody at the table wanted to look a dead fish in the eye. He was seventeen and this was the year he had been assigned the reunion dinner, start to finish, which meant the menu, the timing, the order of dishes, the little speeches. His grandmother had led it for as long as he could remember; his mother had led it the year after his grandmother's stroke; and now, apparently, it was him, because, as his mother put it, "you're the one who cares about food and nobody else in this family can be trusted with a calendar."

Michela was perched on a stool by the window with her phone out, ostensibly helping, actually narrating. "He's holding the fish like it's evidence," she reported to the room. "Exhibit A, one sea bass, deceased."

"Scale it," his grandmother said, handing him the back of a knife, and while he worked, his phone buzzed with the menu draft he'd texted to his mother, now returned with one line deleted and replaced in caps: THE FISH STAYS. He had cut it because it was fussy, because the steaming timing collided with the dumplings, because he had planned something modern and clean, and a whole fish with its head on did not feel modern or clean.

"You look like a lawyer who lost a case," Michela said.

"Everything in this menu is a symbol," Carson said, rinsing scales off his forearms. "The dumplings look like old money. The noodles are longevity, you can't cut them. There's a green vegetable because green sounds like money in Cantonese. I planned all that. And I still almost cut the one thing that actually matters, and I don't know how I missed it."

"Maybe ask the person who's glaring at you," Michela said.

His grandmother was glaring at him, though it was her ordinary glare, the one she used for unswept floors and karaoke. "Yu," she said, tapping the fish. "That is the word for fish. It sounds like the word for surplus. Abundance. You serve fish at the reunion dinner so there is something left over at the end of the year." She said it flat, the way she recited bus schedules, and then went back to lecturing the scallions.

"Wait," Michela said. "The entire dinner is a pun?"

"The entire dinner is a pun," Carson confirmed. "A very old, very serious pun. You can't laugh."

"I would never."

"You're laughing right now."

"I'm laughing incipiently. It hasn't fully arrived yet."

His grandmother snorted, which from her was roughly a standing ovation, and Carson found himself laughing too, scales in his hair, the fish staring up at him with its one dead sincere eye. He had been thinking about the menu all wrong, he realized, not as a list of dishes but as a sentence he was writing for the whole family, and he had nearly written an incoherent one. The modern clean thing, the dumplings shaped like ingots, the uncut noodles, and then no fish, no surplus, nothing carried over into the new year. It would have been like ending a toast halfway through.

"Okay," he said. "Fish stays. Steamed, ginger and scallion, done last so it comes out when everyone's seated. We titrate the soy sauce at the table instead of in the kitchen, so if it's too salty we can still fix it."

"Now he cooks like a chemist," Michela said. "Verrry careful. Add a little, taste, add a little."

"Titrate is the actual word for it," Carson said. "We did it in lab. You add until the color changes."

"Your veracity is overwhelming but your fish is drying out."

He moved the fish to the steamer rack and rearranged the rest of the timeline in his head, pushing the dumplings earlier, the vegetables later, the noodles at the very end so nobody would be too full to finish them. His grandmother watched him renumber the menu taped to the fridge, and when he offered her the pen to check it, she waved it off. "Your dinner," she said, which was either a compliment or a sentence, and left the kitchen.

By seven the relatives were due within the hour and the kitchen smelled like a banquet had detonated in it. Michela had been promoted from narrator to dumpling pleater, badly. Carson set the whole fish, steamed and glistening, on the oval platter in the center of the table, head pointing toward his grandmother's seat because she had told him twice which direction mattered and once that it didn't, and he had decided to believe the version where it did.

The doorbell rang, and the first aunts spilled in with plastic bags of oranges and complaints about parking, and his grandmother took her seat and looked at the fish and then at him, a long inspection.

"Yu," she said.

"Yu," Carson said back, and carried the platter the last inch toward her.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
Anna had promised Mr. Ma a painting of his bakery window by Saturday, and by Thursday evening the shop itself had come out fine, the croissants stacked like little crescent moons, but the light coming through the glass refused to be yellow. It kept looking like margarine. She wanted it to look like morning.

She sat at the kitchen table with her tray of gouache open in front of her, a jar of rinse water going gray beside her elbow. Tenzin had come over to study for the chemistry final and had instead drifted into the kitchen, drawn, as he always was, by other people's projects.

"Add white," he said. "That's what my sister does."

Anna squeezed white into the yellow pool on her palette and stirred. The color went pale and chalky, like a school hallway at three o'clock, and the morning light was gone from it entirely.

"That's worse. That's a dentist's office."

"You could just leave it white," Tenzin said. "The canvas is white. Paper, whatever."

"The paper is white but it isn't light. Light is warm. The whole painting dies if the window looks like a hole." She frowned at the palette. She reached for orange, added a little, then more, then a touch of red for warmth, then some white to lift it back up, then more yellow because the red had dragged it toward brick. She stirred with the back of her brush, and the pool on the palette went a deep, disappointed brown.

"Oh no," Tenzin said, and laughed.

"It's mud." Anna held up the brush and let the mud drip back into the mud. "I added every good color. Orange, red, yellow, white. How is that not the best color? How is the best colors mixed together mud?"

"It's like your locker," Tenzin said. "Everything you like is in there and none of it works together."

Anna laughed despite herself, then stopped laughing, because something was turning over in her head. She remembered Mr. Ma complaining once, querulous and half-joking, about the flour delivery being late: everything piled on everything, he'd said, and somehow you end up with less bread, not more. She looked at the brown pool again. Each paint was doing its own thing, taking something away, and together they took away everything.

"Wait," she said slowly. "Light is the opposite. If you mix lights, colors, like on a screen, they add up brighter. But paint isn't light. Paint is the pigment absorbing stuff. Every pigment I add absorbs more, so mixing a bunch of pigments gets darker and muddier, not whiter. It's going toward brown, not toward light."

"That sounds like a chemistry thing," Tenzin said, "which means it's probably true and also probably on the final."

"It's called subtractive," Anna said. "Paint mixing. I remember Ms. Alper mentioned it in art, like, in passing, and I thought it was a fact for other people." She rinsed her brush and watched the water swirl. "So I can't get to morning by adding. I have to take away."

She got a fresh sheet of palette paper and squeezed out a single clean yellow, bright as an egg yolk, and let it sit there unblended. Then, instead of mixing the window color on the palette, she laid thin strokes side by side on the painting itself, yellow and a whisper of orange, letting the eye of whoever looked at it do the mixing from a distance. The window began to glow. Not like a photograph of morning, but like the memory of one, which was better.

"Two minds," Tenzin said, pointing at the painting and then at her chemistry notes, still open and ignored on the corner of the table. "Art brain and science brain."

"I used to think I had to choose," Anna said. "Like painting was going to emancipate me from school, or school was going to rescue me from being broke. Pick a lane. But the answer was literally sitting in the middle of the palette being brown."

"Deep," said Tenzin. "Also, we have learned nothing for the final."

"We learned one thing for the final. You owe me an hour of quizzing." She wiped her hands on the rag and looked at the finished window for a long moment. "I still don't know if he'll like it. I'm honest about that. He wanted a window, and I gave him an argument about light. That part stays uncertain."

"Then make reparations with a croissant," Tenzin said. "Buy two Friday morning. One for the mistake, one for the masterpiece."

Anna laughed and turned the painting around on the table so the window faced them both, the little strokes of yellow still catching the actual kitchen light, which was, she noticed, nothing like the painted one, and beautiful in an entirely different way.

"Two croissants," she said. "And we tell him nothing about the brown."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
Mia had read the handbook twice on the bus, and the page she remembered was the one about following distance, though she could not have said why it had stuck. At the licensing office she waited in a line that smelled of wet coats and hand sanitizer, clutching her learner's permit the way other people clutched their phones. Nina was ahead of her, half-turned, whispering about the written test she'd just failed on her second try.

"You passed?" Nina said, seeing the paper.

"Barely."

"Malek passed with a hundred. He's an affectation, that's what he is." Nina said it fondly, the way she said everything, and Mia laughed even though she was still shaking a little.

Outside, a gray sedan idled at the curb with a plastic sign on the roof. Mr. Friedman got out. He was the neighbor who had offered the lesson, a retired mail carrier with a flat, unhurried voice, and he had told Mia's mother he would take her out on the quiet streets behind the office before they attempted anything with traffic lights. He walked around the car once, checked the mirrors, and got into the passenger seat. Mia settled behind the wheel and adjusted the seat three times before her feet found the pedals.

The first fifteen minutes went well, or well enough. She turned when he said turn, stopped when he said stop. The trouble came on the straight stretch along the frontage road, where a delivery van sat in front of them doing exactly the speed limit. Mia crept closer. She noticed herself doing it, eased back, and then crept again, as if the van were pulling her on a string. Mr. Friedman said nothing, which was worse than anything he could have said.

"Too close?" she asked.

"How far back do you think you are?"

She looked at the van's bumper, large in the windshield now. "A car length?"

"Watch when the van passes that lamppost ahead. Say 'now' when it does."

She watched, and said "now," and counted, and reached the lamppost almost before she got to two. She hadn't realized. She dropped back, tried again with the next sign, and this time counted a slow one and two that felt like holding her breath. She remembered the handbook then, the page that had stuck, the name for what she was doing. "The two-second rule," she said. "It was on my test." Mr. Friedman grunted, which she took for approval.

The van turned off, and Mia held the gap behind a hatchback instead, counting from mailboxes, from a fire hydrant, from a crack in the pavement where no fixed point should rightly have existed but did. She found she could think while counting, which surprised her. Nina would have said she was being obsessive. Malek would have said something pithy about spatial reasoning and then gotten it wrong himself. Both of them were partly right about her, she thought, and neither was exactly.

Mr. Friedman watched her settle into the distance like someone finding the right volume on a radio. He had taught his daughter thirty years ago, before the arthritis in his hands made him hand over the keys permanently, and he had learned that you could remonstrate with a student or you could give them a lamppost and let the lamppost do the arguing. The lamppost was winning. He reached over and turned the heater down one notch, because the car was getting warm and the girl had enough to think about.

"Turn here," he said. "We'll do the parking lot."

She signaled late, corrected, and swung wide into the lot, counting to two behind a parked sedan that wasn't even moving. She stopped the car, put it in park, and sat with her hands still at ten and two.

"Again Thursday?" Mr. Friedman asked.

"Can we do the road with the lights?"

"After Thursday." He was already out the door, folding the roof sign into the trunk.

Mia stayed in the driver's seat a moment longer, watching the lot's entrance, where a car rolled past the gate and she caught herself counting from the gatepost, one and two, before she realized the car wasn't hers to follow.

Nina was leaning against the office wall near the bus stop, arms crossed against the cold. "How was it?"

"I counted the whole way home," Mia said, and held up her permit. "Quiz me on lampposts."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The festival had taken over four blocks of the street, and Maxime moved through it behind his mother, carrying a paper bag of dumplings that leaked steam onto his wrist. His aunt had assigned him a specific errand before they left home: find his little cousin Benji before the lion dance started and give him the red envelope she had prepared. The envelope sat folded in his jacket pocket, stiff at the corners, and his aunt had been precise about it. Forty dollars, she had said, because Benji had turned ten and because forty was a round, generous number to her, the way it had been at every birthday she could remember.

The smell of fried scallion pancakes drifted from a stall near the corner, where Ms. González from across the street was handing out paper lanterns to kids who could answer questions about the festival. She had lived on their block longer than Maxime had been alive and had apparently appointed herself an informal guide. He had passed her table twice already, and both times he had kept walking, because his mother wanted dumplings and Benji, in that order.

He found Benji first, standing near the folding tables outside the community centre with Alexzander and Maddie from school, who had come for the food and stayed for the drums. Benji was showing them his haul of the afternoon: a paper dragon, a plastic fan, a handful of candy. When Maxime held out the envelope, Benji took it with both hands and immediately began working a finger under the flap.

"Wait," Maxime said, more sharply than he meant to, and Benji froze, suddenly sullen, the way he got whenever anyone older interrupted him. "You're supposed to keep it sealed until later."

"That's not a rule," Benji said, but he said it to the envelope, not to Maxime, and his fingers stayed where they were.

Maddie leaned over Benji's shoulder. "How much?"

"Forty," Maxime said, and something moved at the back of his mind, a fragment from the autumn term, a Tuesday afternoon in a classroom where they had been studying traditions of gift-giving. Ms. González had come in as a guest speaker that day, of all people, with her lanterns and her questions, and the class had gone around the room naming customs. He could not remember who had said it, only the sentence itself, which had stuck because it was short and strange: red-envelope gifts avoid amounts with the number four, because four sounds like the word for death.

"It can't be forty," he said aloud, and Alexzander raised an eyebrow at him, waiting for a reason, which Maxime did not have ready. He looked down the street toward the lantern table, where Ms. González was laughing with a woman holding a toddler. "Hold on," he said, and Benji, obedient for exactly as long as it took Maxime to turn away, slid his finger back under the flap.

The walk to the table took a minute, and Maxime spent it arguing with himself, testing the veracity of a six-month-old memory against the solid fact of the envelope in his aunt's handwriting. She had lived through more of these festivals than he had. She had given red envelopes at every New Year he could remember. But the classroom sentence kept repeating itself with the flat certainty of something copied off a board, and he had written it down, he was almost sure, in the notebook he still kept in his backpack for no reason he could defend.

"Ms. González," he said, reaching the table. "The red envelopes. The money inside. It can't have a four in it, right?"

She set down her lanterns and looked pleased, the way teachers looked when something surfaced months later. "That's right. Four sounds like death. Nobody puts four in one."

He thanked her and walked back, already rehearsing how to say it to Benji without making it sound like a correction of their aunt, and how to say it to his aunt later without making it sound like a correction of Benji. There was no way to hold both loyalties perfectly, he understood that much, and he decided, halfway across the street, that he would give the envelope back to his mother and let her be the one to open it, so that no one had to accuse anyone of anything. Some of it could be handled quietly, and the rest, whatever his aunt said at dinner tonight, would have to be handled then.

Benji had not waited. The envelope was open in his hands, and he was holding the bills up to the festival lights, and Maddie was counting them out loud, and when she reached forty, Benji looked at Maxime with an expression that was half triumph and half a question.

"You want to count them again?" Benji said.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Gar Alperovitz argued in Atomic Diplomacy (1965) that the atomic bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union.
story:
The Cold War gallery on the third floor was nearly empty on a Tuesday afternoon, which was why Mr. Petrov had let them wander up here at all, telling them only to be back at the bus by four. Chase stood in front of a glass case holding a decommissioned missile casing panel, its paint the gray of pencil shavings, while Jia read the wall text out loud in a voice she reserved for things she thought were ridiculous. "The atomic bombings of August 1945 brought the Second World War to its conclusion," she recited. "Last act of the war. Case closed."

"Not closed," Kenley said. He had his phone out, tilted toward the panel as if he might photograph it into agreement. "Last act of World War Two or first act of the Cold War. Those aren't the same story." He had been arguing this since the bus, since before the bus, since Mr. Petrov's lesson on détente three days ago when Kenley had raised his hand and said the whole postwar thing started before the war ended, and Jia had said that was revisionist nonsense, and the two of them had been circling each other ever since.

Chase had mostly stayed out of it, which was unusual for him, because he had been reading something neither of them had. His history teacher, not Mr. Petrov but the one from the seminar he took on Thursdays, had put a photocopied chapter in his mailbox with a sticky note that said only, "For the argument you're not having yet." The chapter was from a book called Atomic Diplomacy, published in 1965, by Gar Alperovitz. He'd read it twice on the bus, the second time with a pencil, and now the pages were dog-eared in his jacket pocket.

"Here's the thing," Chase said, and both of them turned, mildly surprised he was speaking. "There's a historian, Gar Alperovitz. He wrote a book in 1965, Atomic Diplomacy, and he argued the bombs were used on Japan partly to intimidate the Soviet Union." He said it carefully, the way you carry a full glass across a room. "Partly. Not only."

Jia folded her arms. "That's a claim, not a fact." She was good at this distinction, better than he was, and usually he liked that about her. "You can't put a motive in a case the way you put a warhead in a missile." She gestured at the glass.

"You can weigh it, though." Chase pulled out the photocopy, but he didn't open it. Around them the gallery murmured with recorded narration from a nearby screen, and a retired couple moved slowly past a display about the Berlin airlift, an operation whose whole logic, the label said, had been to feed a city without firing a shot. The wartime alliance, another label nearby explained, had been less a friendship than a mutualism, each power needing the other to survive, and the moment the shared enemy began to weaken, the arrangement showed its seams.

"That's the part I keep snagging on," Kenley said, quieter now. "If the alliance was already coming apart, then something like the bomb wasn't just about Japan. It was a message." He looked almost uneasy saying it, as if the idea were too convenient for him. "But that's exactly what makes me suspicious. It fits too well. The story I want to believe fits the evidence like a glove."

Chase nodded, because he'd hit the same wall at one in the morning. Alperovitz's argument adumbrated the whole shape of the decades that followed, the arms race, the mistrust, and that was its power and its problem at once: an explanation that reaches forward and shadows everything can feel true simply because it's large. "The counterweight," he said, "is that Japan was still fighting, and the invasion everyone predicted would have been horrific, and none of Alperovitz's argument makes that go away. Partly. The word does a lot of work." He looked at the missile panel again, at his own incipient reflection surfacing in the glass. "I can't make it more than partly from what I've read. Maybe nobody can."

Mr. Petrov drifted over, hands in his pockets, and stood with them for a moment without saying anything, which was his way of saying plenty. He looked at the case, then at the three of them, then at the photocopied chapter in Chase's hand. "Four o'clock," he said finally. "Bus." And he moved on toward the escalator, leaving the whole disagreement exactly where they'd set it down.

They walked toward the stairs together, the argument not settled but changed, thinner in some places and sturdier in others, like a rope that had been re-spliced. Jia stopped at the display about the airlift and read the label twice. "Mutualism," she said. "Huh. And then it stopped being mutual." Kenley was already composing a post about it, thumbs hovering, but he paused. "So what do we actually say it was? Last act or first act?"

Chase looked back once at the gray panel in its case, at the small placard that had started none of this and settled less. "Say the evidence points both ways," he said. "Say partly. Footnote the rest." Jia snorted, but she was smiling when she pushed open the stairwell door.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A down payment is the part of a home's price the buyer pays upfront so less must be borrowed; in British usage it is called a deposit.
story:
The queue at the bank moved slowly enough that Jaxon had time to reread the brochure three times. He had come in with his mother's rent money in a sealed envelope and instructions to pay it into the landlord's account before noon, and behind that errand a second, quieter purpose: to ask someone official about the flat above Mr. Karimi's shop, the one with the FOR SALE sign that had been there since March. He was eighteen now. He had a job at the garden centre and a savings account with eleven hundred pounds in it, and the sign had begun to feel like a question addressed to him personally.

When his turn came, the adviser behind the desk introduced herself and asked what she could help with. He slid the envelope across first, the simple thing, and watched her count the notes into the machine. Then, before his nerve could desert him, he said he wanted to know about buying a flat. What it actually took. She smiled in the way people smile at puppies barking at mirrors and asked how much he had for a deposit.

"A deposit?" Jaxon said. "I already paid a deposit. On the place we rent now. Five weeks of rent, and you get it back when you leave, if you haven't wrecked anything." He was thinking of the afternoon two years ago when his mother had stood in the empty sitting room of their old flat, counting out the returned deposit in tens and twenties, smoothing each note flat on the kitchen counter before putting it away. That money had bought the secondhand washer and the train tickets to his grandmother's funeral. It had come back to them precisely because they had not been owners, only careful guests.

The adviser's smile flickered, patient but correcting course. She said that for a purchase, the deposit was a different animal, that lenders wanted to see a percentage of the price before they would consider a mortgage, that the larger it was, the better the rates.

Jaxon sat with that. So there were two deposits, the same word pointing in two directions, and the woman at the desk had been using the one that meant money you never saw again, money that went into the price of the thing itself rather than sitting in someone else's account waiting for you to prove you had behaved. He did the arithmetic on the back of the brochure. If the flat above the shop was, say, one hundred and forty thousand, then even the smallest percentage would be thousands, thousands he did not have, and the mortgage would be the difference, borrowed and paid back for decades. He wrote it small, as though writing it small might make it smaller.

Rowan was waiting outside on the wall by the bike racks, eating chips out of the paper with the unselfconscious concentration he brought to everything, including the biology revision he claimed to be doing. When Jaxon told him what had happened, Rowan laughed, not unkindly. "My cousin in Manchester calls it a deposit too. Deposit, down payment, same thing over there, apparently. He just bought a place and won't shut up about it." He offered the chips. "Eleven hundred's a start, though. That's what my dad says about everything. A start."

"It's a fifth of what I'd need for the cheapest flat in town," Jaxon said, "if the cheapest flat in town existed, which it doesn't." He tried to keep it level, not bitter, because bitterness would have made it Rowan's problem to fix and it wasn't. What he wanted, he realized, was not the flat itself but the standing of someone who could be taken seriously in that office, someone whose questions the adviser answered without the flicker. He remembered a film they had watched in English where the teacher praised a performance for its verisimilitude, the quality of seeming true, and he thought that adulthood might be mostly that: performing the part until the paperwork caught up. Mohammed had put it more bluntly once, comparing himself and his brothers in their exam photos, saying genetics had dealt them all the same phenotypic hand and the differences were all in the lighting. Same kid, different frame.

"I'm going to keep saving," Jaxon said, standing, brushing the wall's grit off his hands. "And I'm going to ask Mr. Karimi what he'd actually take for it, because that sign's been up so long the number might not be real anymore." Rowan folded the chip paper into a neat triangle and pitched it at the bin. "And you'll preempt me by asking him before you can be sensible about it, knowing you." Jaxon swung his leg over his bike and looked back once at the bank's glass doors, where the adviser was already leaning toward the next customer. "Probably," he said, and pushed off down the hill toward the shop with the sign.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Landscape architect Ian McHarg's 1969 book Design with Nature promoted stacking maps of soil, water and other factors to decide land use, an idea that GIS later automated.
story:
The laptop slid across the motel bedspread every time Karl shifted his feet, and Tristan kept pulling it back without looking up. On the screen, the city of Carverton was a sprawl of grey parcels, and over it, like a stain spreading through cloth, he had laid the floodplain layer in pale blue. Angie leaned in from the other bed, chewing the last of the gas station pretzels.

"There," she said, pointing at a band where the blue swallowed whole blocks of housing. "That's where Ms. Reyes lives. She was my bus driver in fourth grade."

Tristan zoomed in. The houses inside the flood zone were small parcels, close together, cheaper per the county assessor's layer he'd added that morning. His project for Mr. Aquino's class was due in ten days, and the assignment had seemed abstract until this trip, until Karl's uncle's wedding brought them through Carverton and Angie had said they should stop and see where she used to live. Now the map had a street in it.

They stopped at her grandmother's house the next afternoon, a brick bungalow with a porch swing that squeaked in a wind that never quite stopped. While Angie and the grandmother argued happily about whether the wedding cake had been dry, Tristan wandered to the back room the grandfather had used for his work. The grandfather had died two years ago; the room still smelled of pencil shavings. On a shelf under the window lay a stack of maps on translucent paper, and when Tristan lifted the top sheet, he could see the one beneath it through the paper itself, faint as a ghost.

He carried them to the kitchen table. "What are these?" he asked, and Angie's grandmother wiped her hands on her apron and came to look. "Oh, those are his planning maps. He did that for the county, land use, before computers did everything. He'd draw one thing on each sheet." Tristan laid the sheets one over another, holding them up to the window light. One showed soil. One showed water, creeks and the old marsh edges. One showed where people lived. Stacked, they made a picture none of them held alone, and Tristan stood very still, because he recognized it.

"It's layers," he said. "That's what the software does. That's all it does, really." He told them, half to Angie and half to himself, that he'd read about a landscape architect named Ian McHarg who wrote a book in 1969, Design with Nature, promoting the idea of stacking maps of soil, water and other factors to decide land use, and that GIS later automated it. "The software just does what he did with tracing paper," Tristan said. "He did it by hand. This is his method, right here on this table."

Karl, who had been rummaging in the kitchen for a snack, drifted over and squinted at the stacked sheets. "So your grandfather drew the flood map before there was flooding?" he asked. "Before anybody built there?" The grandmother said the marsh had been drained first and the houses came after, and that everyone had known, in the way a town knows things, and had built anyway, because the land was cheap and the water was quiescent that decade. Tristan thought about that word later, on the porch, watching the creek at the bottom of the yard slide along, low and quiet, giving no sign of anything.

He sat on the swing with his laptop and tried to stack the layers the way the tracing paper had shown him, soil under water under housing, and then reversed it, housing over flood, and the two orderings told two different stories. One said the land had rules. The other said people had ignored them. He wanted to write in his project that the software proved something, that the blue over the parcels was an answer, but the more he moved the layers, the less certain he felt about what the answer was. The map showed where the risk sat; it did not show why a city lets its poorest streets sit inside it. At the wedding rehearsal dinner, a cousin of Karl's uncle had gone on about a populist county commissioner who promised to dredge the creek and fix everything, and Angie had rolled her eyes, and Tristan had said nothing, because he suspected dredging and promises were both maps of a kind, drawn to show whatever the drawer wanted seen.

The next morning they drove out early, the three of them, east toward home. Angie's grandmother had pressed the tracing-paper maps into Tristan's arms at the door and told him to give them to his teacher, so someone would keep them. He held them flat across his knees in the back seat, careful of the creases, and watched Carverton go by outside the window, the streets he now knew from two directions at once. Somewhere past the county line, Angie asked whether he thought his project would win anything.

"Maybe the red layer," Tristan said, and peeled back the top sheet of soil to show the water underneath, blue lines crossing the paper like veins.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
The quiz came back on Tuesday with a red 41 circled at the top, and Seth sat very still while the papers moved down the rows, because Charles-Olivier was already turning around in his seat with his own paper held up like evidence at a trial.

"Eleven out of fourteen," Charles-Olivier said. "Same method as yours. Explain that."

Seth looked at the two papers side by side on the lab bench. The question with the sealed flask of nitrogen and hydrogen, heated from four hundred degrees to five hundred, and then the instruction to recalculate the equilibrium composition. Both of them had carried the old K straight into the new arithmetic, confident as accountants, and both of their answer lines had the same red slash through them.

"I don't explain the marks," Seth said. "I just receive them."

Mr. Jung was at the front writing the word "disturbance" on the board, which he did whenever he wanted the class to feel that chemistry had drama in it. Behind him hung a photograph he had taken himself on some montane trail in Colorado, pine and grey rock and a sky that went on, and Seth had spent portions of the semester looking at it instead of at the board, though today the board was winning.

"Three kinds of disturbance," Mr. Jung said. "You add or remove material. You change the pressure. You change the temperature. Two of these the system absorbs and one it does not. I have said enough. You have twenty minutes of lab time and a partner. Use it."

Adrienne had already opened her notebook to a page with a table ruled into it, four columns, in pencil, because she did not trust pens. "He's telling us one of them is different," she said. "He's telling us with his eyebrows."

"That's a lot of weight for eyebrows to carry," Charles-Olivier said, but he dragged his stool over anyway.

They had the small gas syringes and the sealed tubes of the brown gas, the one that went paler in an ice bath and darker near the warm plate, which had captivated Seth back in September when everything in the course still seemed like magic tricks. He set a tube in the ice bath and they watched the colour fade, and Charles-Olivier copied the observation down, and then Seth moved the same tube to the warm plate and the brown came back, deepened, held.

"Add gas, colour changes," Adrienne said, ruling a row. "Change pressure, colour changes. Heat it, colour changes. Everything changes, Charles-Olivier, I don't know what you want from me."

"Fine," Seth said, but he was not fine. He kept thinking about the quiz, about the arithmetic that had felt so airtight and collapsed anyway. He took out his calculator and the table of constants from the back of the chapter, and he found the row for this reaction, and there were two numbers on it, not one. Two values of K at two temperatures, side by side, as if the table had been quietly saying the thing all semester and nobody had looked.

"Wait," he said. "Look at the table. K at twenty-five degrees, K at a hundred degrees. Different numbers. The same reaction."

Adrienne leaned over. Charles-Olivier leaned over. There was a silence in which the warm plate ticked.

"Temperature is the only one that changes K," Charles-Olivier said slowly, and then he picked up his pen and drew a box around it, hard enough that the pen went through the page, which for Charles-Olivier was an act of grief.

"So on the quiz," Seth said, "we didn't change the composition wrong. We used the wrong constant. The system didn't just shift, it shifted to a different place entirely, a place with different rules."

"Which is why my eleven is unjust," Charles-Olivier said. "I executed the method perfectly."

"You executed a perfectly wrong method," Adrienne said, and ruled another line in her table, and under the column for temperature she wrote "changes K" and under the other two she wrote "doesn't," and she boxed hers in pencil, lightly, so it could be revised.

Seth copied the table into his own notebook and then sat looking at it. He understood what he had gotten wrong, and he understood what the constant meant, but there was something underneath that he could not yet close his hand around, something about how the system could be pushed and pulled and squeezed and stay itself, and then be heated and become a different system with different numbers governing it, and where exactly the old self ended and the new one began. He thought of asking Mr. Jung and decided against it, mostly because Mr. Jung's eyebrows had already done their work.

At the end of the period Mr. Jung collected the syringes and said the retest was Friday. Charles-Olivier raised his hand and began, "Regarding the marking scheme," and Mr. Jung turned to the photograph of the mountains behind him, straightened its corner, and did not answer.

Seth put the notebook away, tube still brown on the warm plate, colour still holding.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
The envelope from the college arrived on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday Gabriella had taped its financial aid letter inside her locker door, the way other people taped photographs. She wanted the laptop more than she had ever wanted anything. The letter offered her a federal loan for the full cost, and beside the cost, in a column labeled "estimated total repayment," sat a number that made her pause. Ricardo leaned over her shoulder in the hallway before first period and said the thing she was already thinking. "That's more than they're giving you."

At lunch her brother called. He was twenty-three, two years out of state college, and he had opened his loan statement in the parking lot at work because he could not wait until his break. His voice had a flattened quality she had only heard once before, the night their father's car was towed. He said he had borrowed twenty-six thousand dollars. He said the balance was now larger than what he borrowed, even though he had been making payments, small ones, and he said, "They told me it's called capitalization. The unpaid interest gets added to the principal, so from then on they charge interest on the interest too." He kept repeating the last part, as if repetition would undo it. Gabriella sat on the bleachers behind the gym with her knees drawn up, phone hot against her ear, saying almost nothing, because he did not seem to want comfort. He seemed to want a witness.

After school she found Ms. Virtanen in the math room, arranging printed worksheets into stacks. Ms. Virtanen had once worked at a credit union; Gabriella had heard this from Arian, who ascribed every useful piece of school gossip to some cousin or other. Ms. Virtanen was reticent about her old job in general, waving off questions with a laugh, but she did not laugh now. "You're asking the right question," she said, "but I'm not going to hand you the answer. There's a reason I keep the formula on the board all semester and it isn't decoration." She pointed at the compound interest expression, the one with the exponent, which had sat ignored above the whiteboard since October. "Start there. Come back when you have something."

Gabriella did not come back alone. She dragged Arian to the library during their free period and spread her brother's numbers across a table, copying them from her phone. Arian wanted to be there even less than he pretended, because he had a philosophy essay due, but he owed her for a semester of calculus help. Ricardo arrived uninvited, sat down, and within minutes had opened a loan calculator on his own phone. He had his own reason: he was financing a camera lens for a side business shooting graduation photos, and until now he had called the monthly payment "basically nothing." He entered numbers, went quiet, and entered them again.

"So the interest they charge each month," Gabriella said slowly, working it out on paper, "if you don't pay it, doesn't just sit there. It joins the principal." She drew an arrow. "And then the interest is charged on that bigger amount. On the interest too." It was the same lemma Ms. Virtanen had made them prove in the fall, dressed in different clothes: compounding, running backward. Ricardo ran the lens calculation a third time and put the phone face down on the table, which in Ricardo's language was a kind of surrender. He had been so cheerful about the lens that morning, describing the shots he would take, the clients he imagined lining up by June.

They stayed until the librarian started stacking chairs. Gabriella wrote a different number on the back of her hand: the amount she could save from the grocery job by August if she kept every shift, small and boring and hers. It would cover half a laptop, maybe, a slower one than the letter promised. Ricardo, sulking, said he would buy the lens secondhand and save the difference instead, though everyone at the table understood he might not, that wanting the lens was its own argument. Arian said something about interest being neither good nor evil, only a tool, and Gabriella told him to save it for his essay.

She was not sure, afterward, that she had arrived anywhere solid. The loan in the letter was still there, still possible, still the fast way to the thing she wanted, and a slower plan could fail too, if her hours got cut or the old laptop died mid-semester. She thought about her brother in the parking lot, and about the same quiet mathematics running in the opposite direction on a savings account, patient and faceless in both cases. That was the part she could not resolve and did not try to: the formula did not care which way you were facing. It only compounded.

On Thursday she stopped at Ms. Virtanen's door with her paper, the arrows, the two numbers side by side. Ms. Virtanen read it through, twice, and set it down. "You found the difference between the two directions," she said. "Most people never look at both." Gabriella folded the paper along its crease and put it in the pocket with the college envelope. "I'm going to the bank on Saturday," she said. "I want to see what a savings account pays before I sign anything." Ms. Virtanen pulled a chair up to her desk. "Sit down first. Bring your pen."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A poll's stated margin of error applies to each candidate's share; the margin of error for the lead between two candidates is about twice as large.
story:
At 9:14 on a Tuesday night, Jaxon's phone buzzed against his desk, and the group chat surfaced on his screen. It was called "gov club minus bouchard," a name Maximus had chosen in September and refused to change even though it had started to feel like an obsolescent joke, the kind of thing that was funny for a week and then just sat there. Maximus had posted a link to a poll about the school board election with the caption "IT'S OVER. Nguyen by 4. pack it up."

Elie replied three minutes later, in the rapid-fire style she used when she was doing homework with the chat open beside her. "4 point lead is basically a blowout." Then, "margin of error is 3 so even at worst she's up 1." Jaxon read it twice. He was supposed to be finishing his chemistry lab, and the paragraph about reaction rates sat half-written under the chat window, but something about Elie's arithmetic bothered him in a way he couldn't immediately delimit. The feeling had edges he couldn't locate yet, so he typed "wait" and then, before he could decide what came after it, Maximus sent a string of trophy emojis.

Jaxon set the phone face down and picked up a pencil. On the back of his lab handout he wrote the numbers the way Elie had framed them: Nguyen at 51, Reyes at 47, margin of error 3. He wrote "worst case for Nguyen: 48" and "best case for Reyes: 50." Then he stopped. The two numbers were not the same, and they weren't even on the same side of the line. Reyes's best case beat Nguyen's worst case by two. He crossed out "up 1" and wrote a question mark over it, and the question mark looked more correct than anything else on the page.

He typed into the chat: "elie how did you get up 1." Her answer came as a screenshot of a sticky note, her handwriting slanting hard to the right: 51 - 3 = 48, 47 stays, difference still 1. "you only subtract from one of them," she wrote, "the leader." Jaxon stared at it. He could see why it seemed right, the way a contrivance always seems right until you check what it's actually doing, and it occurred to him that subtracting from only one candidate was like weighing a truck by removing cargo from one side of it. "but the poll doesn't know which number is off," he sent. "the error is on the whole poll."

Maximus sent "bro it's ONE poll question are we really doing math at 9pm." Jaxon said yes. He opened the polling site itself and scrolled past the headline numbers to the section underneath, the fine print most people never reached, and read it with his thumb hovering over the keyboard. When he found the sentence he was looking for, he read it three times to make sure he wasn't inventing it, then took a screenshot and dropped it into the chat without comment. The screenshot said that the margin of error applied to each candidate's share, and that the margin of error for the lead between the two candidates was about twice as large.

The chat went quiet for almost a minute, which in this chat was a geological age. Then Elie sent "oh." Then, "so a 4 point lead with a 3 point margin of error isn't a sure thing at all. the lead's own margin is like 6." Maximus sent a single "hm," and Jaxon watched the typing indicator appear and disappear twice, which meant Maximus was composing and deleting, composing and deleting. Finally: "so it could basically be a tie." Jaxon wrote "or a real lead. we can't tell them apart with this one poll. that's the whole problem."

Elie's next message took longer. "ok but the article says IT'S OVER." Jaxon pulled the article back up. The headline was in forty-point font and the margin of error was in eleven-point font at the bottom, and he thought about how the two type sizes were making a claim together, one loud and one quiet, and how most readers only ever met the loud one. He didn't type any of that. He typed "the headline's not wrong exactly. it's just answering a different question than the one we asked."

Maximus's reply came in lowercase, which for him meant sincerity: "so what do we tell people at the meeting tomorrow." Jaxon looked at his chemistry lab, still half-finished, and then at the screenshot sitting in the chat like a small flat stone with the actual numbers under it. He typed "tell them it's close. tell them the poll can't settle it." Elie sent a thumbs up. Then, a second later, separately, as if she'd thought of it after: "and that a 4 point lead with a 3 point margin of error could go either way, because the lead's margin is about double." Jaxon locked his phone and turned back to the reaction rates, and outside his window a car went by with its brights on in the middle of the block.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
story:
The line at the bank moved slowly, and Sebastian spent the wait rereading the flyer for the summer landscaping crew, which required, in bold letters near the bottom, a driver's license and reliable transportation, both due by Monday. He had the license. He had eleven hundred dollars saved, the deed to nothing, and his mother's old Corolla was dead in the driveway with a cracked head, a phrase the mechanic had delivered like a diagnosis.

He'd arranged to meet Elaina here because she had done this before, or claimed to. She worked Saturdays at the credit union across town and had strong opinions about banks, which she aired in a low, amused voice while they inched forward. "They'll try to sell you the payment," she said. "Not the car. The payment. Watch."

The loan officer, a tired man whose name tag read Mr. Sánchez, pulled up a listing on his monitor for a used hatchback, six thousand dollars, and laid out the arithmetic on a printed sheet. At the interest rate Sebastian qualified for, five years meant a monthly payment Sebastian could just cover between shifts. Then Mr. Sánchez tapped the keyboard. "Or," he said, "we can go seven years. The payment drops considerably." He slid the second sheet across, and the number was beautiful, small enough to feel like almost nothing.

Sebastian stared at it. Then he ran his finger down to the total line at the bottom of each sheet, the full amount he would pay back over the life of the loan, and sat still for a moment. The longer term had a smaller payment and a bigger total. He looked up. "So I'd be paying more overall. Every month is easier, but the whole thing costs more."

"That's the trade," Mr. Sánchez said, and left it there, watching him with what might have been approval or simple patience.

Behind them a man in a paint-spattered jacket began, loudly, to excoriate a teller about a hold on a check, calling the policy theft, calling it worse, and the branch manager drifted over to absorb it. Sebastian tuned it out. He was doing the subtraction on the folder's margin, the difference between the two totals, and the number he got was roughly the cost of the head gasket that had killed the Corolla. Money he would hand over for nothing except the feeling, month to month, of being comfortable.

"I think people take the long one," Elaina said, not unkindly. "Everybody takes the long one. My cousin took an eight-year loan on a truck." She paused. "He still owes on it and the truck's already falling apart."

"It's not an affectation, taking the short one," Sebastian said, and immediately regretted the word, because it wasn't the word he meant; he meant it wasn't a pose, a performance of responsibility for an audience of one bank officer. Elaina raised an eyebrow anyway. He felt his ears go hot. "I mean. If I take the five-year, I'm done when I'm twenty-three. If I take the seven, I'm twenty-five."

The afternoon light through the branch windows had gone torpid and gold, and the queue behind them had grown. Somewhere a printer was churning. Sebastian thought about his savings account, the eleven hundred, which the bank had been quietly adding to each quarter, small deposits he'd never noticed until he checked the statement in the lobby. Interest working for him there, interest working against him here, the same mechanism pointed in opposite directions. He said, "Five years."

Mr. Sánchez nodded and began filling in the forms. He mentioned, without looking up, that if Sebastian kept automatic transfers going to the savings account, the interest there would compound at the same steady rate it always had, and Sebastian nodded as though he'd known that all along, though he had only understood it forty minutes earlier.

Walking out with the approval letter folded in his jacket, Sebastian checked his phone: three texts from Hasan, who knew a guy selling a trailer for the landscaping crew, two hundred dollars, first come first served by tonight. Elaina read over his shoulder. "You have two hundred?"

"After the down payment, yeah. Barely." He stood on the bank steps doing the math a last time, the payment he'd signed for against the wages he hadn't yet earned, the trailer against whatever came after the trailer. Somewhere in there he would be short in August, probably, and he couldn't say how much. He put the phone in his pocket and held the door for Elaina. "Call Hasan," he said. "Tell him we're coming."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS data comes in two main forms: vector data uses points, lines and polygons, while raster data is a grid of cells, each holding one value.
story:
The laptop took three tries to connect to the Wi-Fi, because her grandmother's router had the idiosyncrasy of working only when it faced the kitchen window, and nobody had ever explained why. Camille balanced it on the sill anyway, between a jar of igneous-looking candy her grandmother swore was fudge, and opened the map project she'd been assigned for the summer bridge program. The task was simple to state and slippery to do: overlay a map of flood risk onto a map of housing in the city, and write about which neighborhoods sat inside the hazard zones. Her grandmother's street, it turned out, was one of them.

She had two files. The housing file, when she loaded it, showed up as clean shapes: little polygons for each parcel, sharp-edged, each one carrying an address and a year built. The flood file loaded as something completely different, a wash of tiny colored squares, like a photograph of the city taken from very far away and then zoomed past the point of sense. When she layered them, the shapes and the squares argued. She couldn't click a flood cell and ask which house it belonged to, because it didn't belong to any house. It belonged to itself.

"You look like you're trying to sublimate the printer," her grandmother said from the doorway, meaning glare at it until it vanished into gas. She set down a glass of iced tea Camille hadn't asked for and would drink anyway.

"It's the data," Camille said. "One map is shapes and the other one's, like, pixels. I don't know which one is wrong."

She called Deegan, who had finished his project in what he described as "a heroic eleven hours" and was insufferable about it in the way of someone who had also cried at hour nine. He picked up on the second ring, his ceiling behind him.

"Let me guess," he said. "Your flood map looks like a bad screenshot."

"How did you know?"

"Because I spent half of Thursday thinking I'd broken the software. I didn't. Neither did you." There was the sound of him eating something. "The shapes are vector. Vector data uses points, lines and polygons. The pixel thing is raster, and raster is a grid of cells, each one holding a single value. Flood risk comes as raster. Housing comes as vector. They're just two different ways of storing a map."

Camille wrote this on the back of a utility envelope, because her notebook was in her duffel and her duffel was a problem for Monday Camille. "So one of them isn't broken."

"Neither of them is broken. You have to convert, or sample, or something. Honestly I stopped understanding at 'convert' and just clicked the button with the most reassuring name."

She laughed, and he described the button, which was called something with the word "zonal" in it, and she found it, and it worked the way he said, mostly. Mostly meant that when the flood layer slid over her grandmother's block, the color sat halfway across the polygons like a tide that couldn't decide. One half of a parcel was in the zone. The other half was out. The cell that covered her grandmother's roof also covered the Sandovals' driveway next door, one value stretched across two lives, and the software would not tell her which of them the value was really about.

Mr. Doyle, the neighbor who had lived on the street longer than anyone, came over that evening to return a casserole dish, and Camille, more to be polite than anything, showed him the map on her screen. He put on his glasses. He studied the boundary running through his own backyard with the expression of a man being shown his own X-ray.

"That line's wrong," he said, tapping the glass. "The water came to the shed in '09. Not the fence. The shed."

"The data doesn't go finer than this," she said. "Each square is one value for everything inside it."

"Then the square is wrong."

She nodded, because he was right, and because the software was also right, and because these were two kinds of right that did not stack. She thought about writing that in her report, that the map told the truth at one size and Mr. Doyle told it at another, and that she hadn't yet found the tool that could hold both. She wasn't sure such a tool existed, or whether it should. Some uncertainties you reported; some you just carried.

She worked until the window went dark and the router, faithful to its own private logic, cut out. Her grandmother drifted past in her robe, paused at the screen, and pointed at the blue-green wash covering half the street.

"That's the flood," Camille said.

"I know what it is, baby. I've been swimming in it." Her grandmother tapped the polygon with the reading glasses, once, on the house that was hers. "Make sure you get my side of the square."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
story:
The co-op placement had put Chase at a logistics company two bus transfers from his school, where he spent Thursday mornings filing delivery receipts and, as his supervisor put it, "learning how an office actually runs." What Chase wanted, more than he had admitted on the application, was a reference letter strong enough to matter on a college application, and by the third week he had begun to suspect that the letter would only be as good as the work anyone could actually remember him doing.

That Thursday, the warehouse coordinator, a sullen man who spoke mostly to the printer, shoved a laptop toward him and said, "The student can type. Type this." He then dictated, over eleven minutes, an email to the regional manager about a delayed shipment of compressors: an apology, a weather anecdote, a complaint about the freight company, another apology, and somewhere in the middle, almost inaudible, a request that the manager approve renting a van for two days to move the stock from the secondary depot. Chase typed all of it, read it back, and felt his stomach drop. The request, the only part that needed answering, was buried in paragraph four.

"Should I send it like that?" he asked.

"Send what I said," the coordinator said, and went to argue with the printer.

Chase sat with the email open, cursor blinking after the words "as I may have mentioned, the weather in March." He remembered, suddenly and uselessly, his father at the kitchen table last winter, reading a letter from the insurance company aloud, hunting through four paragraphs of courtesies for the sentence that said what they would actually pay. His father had ascribed it to bad faith, that burying, but Chase had wondered even then whether it was just habit, nobody having been taught any other way. Now he was the one typing the buried sentence, and it felt less like bad faith than like a mistake nobody had named yet.

He pulled out his phone under the desk and texted Shay, who was doing a co-op at an army reserve unit and complained about it constantly. Shay replied in forty seconds: "we literally get drilled on this. it's called BLUF, Bottom Line Up Front, a US military writing standard. main point or request goes in the first lines, before the supporting details. rewrite it that way and my sergeant would actually read it."

Chase deleted the weather anecdote first, which hurt a little, because it was the best-written part. He typed a new opening: "Request: approval to rent a van for two days to transfer compressors from the secondary depot." Then the delay, one sentence. Then the freight company issue, one sentence. Then the apology, shortened until it sounded professional rather than grovelling. When he printed a draft for the coordinator, the man read it standing up, took less than a minute, and said, "Huh. Fine." That was the closest thing to praise Chase had heard from him in three weeks.

The reply came back before lunch: approved, and a second line Chase read three times. "Whoever wrote this, have them do the weekly reports." The coordinator looked at him across the partition. "You did that?"

"Restructured it," Chase said. "The request, first."

"The what?"

"The request, up front." Chase did not say the acronym again. He had learned it an hour ago from a text message, and he was honest enough with himself to know he had applied a rule without fully understanding when it stopped being the right one; there had been, after all, something human in the coordinator's rambling version, an apology that felt like an apology. He wasn't sure yet whether that something was worth keeping in business writing or whether it belonged only in letters read aloud at kitchen tables. He put the uncertainty away for later, the way he filed receipts, in a place he could find again.

The regional manager came through the office the following Thursday, a woman with reading glasses pushed into her hair, and stopped at Chase's desk. "You're the van email," she said. "Do you know Penelope, from the co-op at the legal clinic? She sent me something similar last month. Recommendation letter level, both of you, if you keep it up." Chase said thank you, and meant it, and after she moved on he caught the coordinator almost smiling at the printer.

At the end of the placement there would be paperwork, a form asking what he had learned, and Chase already knew he would not ascribe his improvement to talent or luck. He thought of the recompense the email had earned him, not money but something exchanged all the same, and of his father's insurance letter, and of Shay's sergeant somewhere reading the first lines of everything. He opened a new document, titled it Weekly Report, and typed the main point first.

"Approved for filing," the coordinator said behind him. "Two copies."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
story:
Anthony had the poster taped above his desk, a print of The Two Fridas he'd bought at the museum shop in September, and for three weeks he had looked at it the way he looked at most things: sideways, while doing something else. The assignment was due Friday. Mr. Rivera had written on the board, "Formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism. Not biography. Not feelings. The painting itself." Then he had underlined the last sentence twice, which was as close as he got to shouting.

Cheyenne had already finished hers, apparently in one sitting, and had texted him a photo of her opening paragraph with the caption "ez." Anthony found this almost as infuriating as the assignment itself, because his own draft was two sentences long and both of them were lies. He had written that the painting was "powerful" and "deeply personal," which was exactly the kind of thing Mr. Rivera had told them not to write.

He pulled his desk lamp closer and tried to look at the poster as if he had never seen it before. Two women sat side by side on a green bench, holding hands. One wore a white European dress, its lace torn open at the chest to expose a broken heart, veins snipped by surgical forceps, a single drop of blood traveling down the white fabric. The other wore the Tehuana dress, the warm reds and golds of it, her heart whole, her hand holding a small portrait that a vein connected back to her body. Above them, a storm-grey sky. Below, a cracked, dry earth.

He got out his notebook and started with what he could count. The two figures filled the canvas almost entirely, seated with their skirts spread wide, so that the eye went left to right and then back, left to right, like a pendulum. Why two? Why the same face twice? He wrote the question down without answering it. It felt more honest than pretending.

His phone buzzed. Josephine.

"Are you doing the Kahlo thing," she said, not quite a question.

"Attempting it. Failing at it. You?"

"Done, mostly. Want to compare? Also I have actual images on my laptop, way better than a poster."

"Come over. My mom's making soup, there'll be enough."

She arrived twenty minutes later with her laptop under her arm and an acerbic review of the soup, which she ate two bowls of. Then they spread out on the living room floor, because the light was better there, and she opened a high-resolution image side by side with a diagram she'd found.

"So here's the thing I got wrong," she said. "I kept writing about it like it was a normal portrait size. Then I actually checked. It's huge. It's a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side."

Anthony sat back on his heels. "That's taller than me."

"Almost exactly as tall as you, actually. Two seated self-portraits side by side, and they still fill the whole square. That's the composition. That's your analysis right there."

He stared at the poster, then at the screen, then at the poster again, and something shifted, the way a word looks different once you learn it has a second meaning. He had been looking at a print. The real thing was a room you stood in front of, the two figures nearly life-sized, their joined hands at the exact center of a square, which meant the painting balanced on that small clasp of fingers. The European Frida's forceps, the blood, the storm sky, all of it arranged around a central axis of connection.

"Wait," he said. "That's why the symmetry matters. In a rectangle you'd read it like a story, left to right. In a square it's more like a scale. Two sides, and the middle is where they're weighed."

"Ooh," Josephine said. "Steal that. No, wait, I'm stealing that."

"Joint custody," Anthony said, and pulled his notebook over. He wrote fast, half-formed: the cold palette of the left Frida, white and grey and the thin red line of blood, against the warm earth of the right, and how the sky apportionment, the clouds clustered darker above the torn heart, made the sadness uneven, not mirrored but answered.

"But you still can't do symbolism without biography," Josephine said, chewing her pen. "Rivera said not biography, but the portrait in her hand is Diego. That's a fact about her life, not just the painting."
