It offended some instinct in her, the same instinct that believed effort and reward moved in lockstep, that if she studied twice as hard her marks climbed twice as high. Maybe they didn't. Maybe everything that mattered ran on squares: small excesses compounding quietly into large ones. She thought of Clara, who had gone from texting her daily to texting her monthly, so gradually that Isabelle hadn't noticed the slope until the friendship was a different thing entirely. She thought of her mother's malaise since the spring, which everyone called tiredness because tiredness could be slept off.

"The problem," Mr. Joseph said, interrupting nothing so much as her own silence, "isn't that drivers don't know the numbers. It's that the numbers don't feel like anything at twenty. You have to decide in advance what you believe, and then drive like you believe it." He opened his door and stepped out onto the driveway, leaving hers running. "Back it in. Straight this time."

She watched the fence post in the mirror, the one she'd kissed an hour ago, and backed in slow, correcting an inch at a time, and when she set the brake the car sat square between the rosebushes, almost perfect. It was a small thing, a driveway-sized thing, and it cost her the whole of her attention for five minutes, which was maybe the point. She still didn't know whether to trust a world where effects outran their causes, where doubling down anywhere could quadruple the reckoning. But she knew the number now, and numbers, unlike everything else this year, stayed where you put them.

She cut the engine and sat with her hands still on the wheel. Out on the sidewalk, Leandre was walking past with his backpack slung wrong off one shoulder, and he stopped at the end of the driveway and called out, "Did you drive that?"

"Twice," she called back, "the whole block." She held up the keys so they caught the late light, and Mr. Joseph, already halfway to his own car, turned and gave her a single approving nod.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
The printout covered the gym bench in front of Parker like a failed map. Monday: 400 meter repeats. Tuesday: 400 meter repeats. Wednesday: 400 meter repeats, because Wednesday had seemed like a Tuesday when he wrote it. Somewhere near the bottom, in handwriting that betrayed his confidence, he had added the word REST and crossed it out twice.

"Coach wants our weekly plans by Friday," he said to Theresa, who was lacing her spikes two benches over. "Mine is a wall of running with no doors in it."

Theresa leaned over and studied the page. "You've got no warm-up either. You wrote 'run' for every day, including Sunday, and Sunday is when the mall opens."

"That's not a warm-up. That's a life." But he folded the paper along a crease he'd already worn soft, which meant he knew she was right.

The trial run happened Thursday after last bell, on the track behind the school with the wind coming off the bleachers. Parker had decided to test his plan on Eve-Marie, who ran the 100 and was, in his private accounting, the fastest human he knew. She agreed with an ebullient enthusiasm that should have warned him. Before the first sprint, she did what she always did: dropped into a stretch at the start line and held it, counting slowly, one minute at least for each leg, sometimes longer, rocking gently with her eyes closed like someone praying for speed.

He put her through his program anyway. Two 150s, timed, then a rest, then two more. Her split times came back and Parker read them twice, because they were worse than her times from Monday, when she'd merely jogged a lap and gone straight to the line. She was flat. She felt it too, standing with her hands on her hips, frowning at the finish line as though it had moved.

"That's the third slow one," she said. "My legs feel like they belong to somebody's grandmother."

Parker sat on the infield with his clipboard and did not write anything for a while. In chemistry, Ms. Vogel had a phrase she used when someone gave an answer built to avoid being wrong: "That's a circumlocution, not a conclusion." He could hear her saying it now about his whole plan. He had filled the week with the appearance of work and called it training. He thought about Eve-Marie on the start line, holding those long stretches, and about how she'd gone out sluggish and stayed sluggish, and something assembled itself in his head, clumsy but load-bearing.

"Okay," he said. "I think it's the stretching."

Eve-Marie sat down beside him, suddenly interested. "Stretching makes me slow?"

"Long holds, right before you go," Parker said. "Static stretches, about sixty seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive stuff. They can briefly reduce your strength and power. That's why programs warm up with dynamic movement instead." He was careful with the words, the way he was careful when repeating a formula he hadn't yet earned.

"So leg swings, walking lunges, stuff like that," Eve-Marie said. "Not the praying thing."

"The praying thing can happen after." He wrote it down. Friday on the rebuilt page began with dynamic warm-up in his small blocky capitals. Monday became repeats; Tuesday became something easy; Wednesday, resurrected from the dead, said REST in ink heavy enough to hold it down. Thursday was fast work again, and Sunday, surrendered, said nothing at all.

They tested it the following week, same track, same wind. Eve-Marie swung her legs at the line, did her lunges, joked too loudly about grandmothers, and then ran a 150 that was faster than any of Thursday's. Parker clicked the watch and felt something in him metabolize the moment, turn it into fuel and structure, though he could not have said what exactly had changed in him versus what had only changed in the paper.

Later, in the emptying corridor, Theresa caught him at the water fountain and asked whether the plan had worked. Parker told her the times, both days, in order, and let her do the comparing. Then he stood holding his clipboard against his chest.

"It worked once," he said. "One afternoon, one person. Maybe it was the wind. Maybe she was just tired last week."

"So you don't know yet."

"I know enough to try it again." He hoisted his bag. "Ask me in three Sundays."

He pushed through the doors into the lot, where the light had gone long and low across the buses, and began to run, easily, at the pace the page now prescribed for days like this one.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Galileo showed that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola, in his book Two New Sciences, published in 1638.
story:
Carson set the garden hose nozzle to jet and held it at shoulder height, aiming across the backyard toward the fence. The water rose, hung for an instant, and fell into the grass in a curve he had seen before, two nights ago, on page 112 of his physics textbook, though he had not understood it then.

The test was Monday. Ms. Wiśniewski had written two words on the board before the bell, horizontal and vertical, and underlined both, and said only, "They do not know about each other." Then she had assigned twelve problems and left the room, which was her way of teaching, and half the class was lost. Corbin had texted him that morning: my dad says just memorize the formulas. Corbin's dad was lionized in their neighborhood for having once done engineering, and Corbin repeated his pronouncements as though they were laws.

Carson had come out here because memorizing had failed him twice already on the practice test. He uncapped a marker he had taken from the kitchen, knelt, and drew the water's arc on the patio concrete, freehand, then went back over it until the line was dark. It looked like the graphs from class. It looked like something older, too, and he could not place what.

Alyssia let herself in through the side gate, as she always did, holding the practice test folded into a small square. "You're drawing on your patio," she said.

"I'm checking something." He turned the nozzle to a wider spray and then back to jet, tilting it higher. The water reached farther before falling. "Watch. If I aim it up more, it goes farther until a certain angle, then less far. That's the range equation. But the shape never changes." He traced the new arc in the air with his finger. "It's always this."

"That's the whole thing?" Alyssia sat on the step and unfolded her test. Her score was circled in red at the top, and she kept her thumb over it. "Because I can do the vertical part. Things go up, things come down, gravity, nine point eight. It's the horizontal part that's wrong somehow. Every time."

"That's what I keep getting wrong too," Carson said. He was quiet for a second, working it through out loud, slowly. "I think I've been treating it like one motion. Like the water knows it's falling and decides to slow down sideways. But it doesn't. The sideways part just continues, same speed the whole time, while the vertical part does its own thing. Two separate problems wearing one curve."

Alyssia pulled the cap off the marker and wrote on the concrete under his arc, splitting it with a vertical line, then another, then another, cutting the curve into slices. "So at each slice, the horizontal step is the same width," she said. "Only the vertical gaps change. Small, big, big, small." She looked at it, then at him. "When did you figure this out?"

"Just now. Sort of." He aimed the hose again, lower this time, almost flat, and the water hit the fence in a fast, shallow bow. "There's a book," he said. "It was in the margin next to the chapter. Two New Sciences. Galileo proved a projectile follows exactly this shape, a parabola. Published in 1638." He said the year the way you say a year you have just learned and do not yet trust. "Somebody drew this same arc almost four hundred years ago, except probably not with a hose."

From the porch, Ms. Wiśniewski, who was renting the upstairs apartment and had come down for her mail, said, "It's past six, Carson. Your mother asked me to remind you about dinner." She was a querulous woman in general, and everyone on the street knew it, but her tone softened when she saw the concrete. She stood a moment looking at the marked-up arc and the sliced parabola and the wet grass. "In my day we used a faucet in the lab," she said. "Physiology, physics, all of it came through the hands." Then she took her mail and went back up the stairs.

Alyssia was already copying the sliced curve into her notebook, numbering the slices, checking with a ruler that the horizontal widths matched. "I still don't get why the angle for maximum distance is forty-five degrees," she said. "Or why my answer to problem seven came out negative. Some of it's still just shapes to me."

"Me too," Carson said. He turned off the hose and stood there dripping, the marker still in his hand, looking at the curve drying paler and paler on the concrete.

"Draw it one more time before it disappears," Alyssia said. "And this time label the axes."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
story:
The hayloft smelled of dust and warm alfalfa, and Nicolas had spread his biology notes across a plank laid over two bales because the farmhouse kitchen belonged to his mother's canning project until sundown. He was supposed to be explaining transcription and translation aloud, a study trick Ms. Munro had recommended, and he had invited Pascal and Lachlan out to the farm partly to practise on them and partly because neither of them could say no to free riding lessons in the afternoon. The textbook lay open to a diagram of DNA unzipping, RNA polymerase crawling along one strand, messenger RNA peeling away and traveling to the ribosome, where codons were read three letters at a time and matched to amino acids until a protein hung complete from the assembly line.

"You're going too fast," Pascal said. He was lying full length in the loose hay, boots crossed, and his nonchalant posture made Nicolas unreasonably annoyed, since Pascal could recite the whole chapter without appearing to have opened it. "Slow down at the part where the letters become the protein. That's where I get lost."

Lachlan, sitting on the plank's edge with his cap pushed back, had his own agenda entirely. He wanted to see the new foal before they did anything else, and he kept glancing at the barn door as if the mare might walk past it on her own. Nicolas had promised him the foal after one full explanation, a bargain Lachlan had accepted with the weary patience of someone who suspected he was being titrated, his enthusiasm carefully measured out drop by drop to keep him studying.

Nicolas started over, tracing the diagram with his finger. DNA stays in the nucleus like a master copy in a vault. Transcription makes a working photocopy, the messenger RNA, and carries it out to the ribosome. Then translation, where the ribosome reads the copy in three-letter words and snaps together the right amino acid for each word. He had it memorized well enough to say it in his sleep, which was exactly what worried him, because memorized things had a way of dissolving under exam pressure.

Then Pascal, idly flipping pages, stopped at a practice problem and frowned. "This one has to be a misprint." He held the book up. "They change one letter in the DNA, show you the new codon, and the finished protein comes out exactly the same. Same amino acid, same everything. How can you change the instruction and nothing changes?"

Nicolas looked at it. The original codon was one triplet, the mutated one another, and when he traced each through the chart at the back of the book, both triplets pointed to the same amino acid. His first instinct was that the book was wrong; his second was slower and stranger. Two different words, the same meaning. He sat with that for a moment, running his thumb along the page. "They're synonyms," he said finally. "Different codons, same amino acid. So changing that one base doesn't change the protein at all."

Pascal sat up out of his sprawl, hay in his hair. "There's a name for that, I think. I saw it in the margin somewhere. Silent mutations. The change happens but the protein never notices."

They tested it against other codons, picking triplets at random from the chart and hunting for pairs that led to the same amino acid. Some changes broke the protein; some changed one amino acid for another; and some, like the first, changed nothing. Nicolas wrote the three cases in the margin of his notes in his cramped hand, and it occurred to him that the cell's system was like a language with redundancy built in, forgiving of small errors, not brittle. He thought of his grandfather, who ran the farm before his uncle did, and of a July years ago when the old man had let six-year-old Nicolas help with the haying. Even then he had understood that you did not grab every stray stem; you raked the windrow in one direction and let the baler take what it took, and what the field lost to scatter did not ruin the winter's feed. A system that could absorb small losses without failing. He had not known the word for it then and he did not need one now.

"Is it a flaw or a safety feature?" Lachlan asked, leaning over the chart. He had given up pretending not to be interested. "I mean, if the cell copies billions of letters, it's going to make mistakes. Maybe most mistakes just don't matter."

"Or maybe they matter later, somewhere we can't see yet," Pascal said. He sounded, for once, less certain than usual, and Nicolas liked him better for it. Nicolas admitted he couldn't decide either. He had come out to the loft believing the subject was a set of steps to be recited, and now it seemed more like an argument the cell was constantly having with entropy, order defended against error, imperfectly. He closed the book around his finger to hold the page.

The light through the slats had gone long and amber, and somewhere below a gate clinked. Lachlan was already on his feet. "Foal," he said, and took the ladder two rungs at a time.

Nicolas followed him down into the evening barn, the chart of codons still open in his mind like a map of a country where several roads led to the same city. Pascal came last, carrying the textbook, and handed it over without a word as they crossed the yard. In the far stall the mare lifted her head, and beside her the foal stood on legs it had not yet learned to trust, wobbling once, then steadying, then wobbling again.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make.
story:
Charlotte had the kitchen table to herself until five, which was the only reason the worksheet had a chance. The problem read: given 48 grams of magnesium and plenty of hydrochloric acid, how many moles of hydrogen gas form. She had copied the molar mass of magnesium onto her palm during sixth period, twenty-four point three, and now she wrote it on the worksheet before she could sweat it off.

The first step was the one Ms. Harper had drilled until it felt like a reflex. Grams of reactant divided by grams per mole gives moles of reactant. Charlotte set it up, forty-eight over twenty-four point three, and got just under two moles. That part she trusted. The trouble came after, where the equation said one mole of magnesium produced one mole of hydrogen, and she could not tell whether she was supposed to multiply, divide, or simply stare at it until it confessed.

The front door banged and Rhiannon came through it holding a grocery bag, which she set on the counter with the ceremony of someone who had walked four blocks in the wind for it. "Bread, peanut butter, jelly," she announced. "Walker's coming over after his shift and he's always starving, so I figured we'd make sandwiches before the chem test instead of studying for it."

Charlotte pulled two slices from the loaf and reached for the jar. Rhiannon, who had a system, laid out eight more slices in rows. "He eats like four minimum," she said. Then she checked the jar of peanut butter, tipped it, and frowned. "There's enough peanut butter for maybe three sandwiches. I got the big loaf by happenstance, it was the last one and it was cheap, but the jar's nearly empty." She looked honestly stricken, as though Walker might arrive destitute and leave betrayed.

Charlotte stopped with the knife halfway to the bread. The arithmetic was sitting right there on the counter. Plenty of bread, not enough peanut butter, and the sandwiches stopped when the peanut butter did. "Oh," she said. "Oh, that's the thing. Ms. Harper's problem from Tuesday. The bread could make six sandwiches but the peanut butter only makes three, so the peanut butter decides. It's called the limiting reactant." Rhiannon raised an eyebrow at the word but kept spreading, and Charlotte watched her do it, jar scraping, thinking that the worksheet had never once smelled like peanuts.

She went back to the table and looked at her numbers again. Not enough of one thing, plenty of another, and the smaller amount capped the whole reaction. In her problem there was only one reactant given with a mass, so the magnesium had to be the one that ran out first, the one that set the greatest amount of product the reaction could make. Two moles of magnesium in, two moles of hydrogen out. She wrote the answer and then, because she did not trust herself, wrote it again beside it in smaller handwriting, the way a person double-knots a shoelace.

"I still don't get why we couldn't just buy more peanut butter," Rhiannon said, bringing over a plate with the three finished sandwiches. "You're the one who spent your money on bread."

"I thought more bread was better," Charlotte said. "More of anything seemed better. But it wasn't the thing that mattered." She turned the worksheet toward her friend. "See, I was going to multiply by the acid too, like it all counts. But the acid isn't even measured in the problem. It's just there, like the bread."

Walker arrived with his backpack still on one shoulder and his hoodie smelling faintly of the coffee shop, and he ate two of the three sandwiches in the time it took Charlotte to explain what she had figured out. He listened with the particular patience of the genuinely hungry, then pointed his crust at the worksheet. "So for the test, I find which one runs out first and that one tells me the most product I can get?"

"That one," Charlotte said, and slid the page across so he could see the setup, the division, the clean two moles at the end. Rhiannon went to the pantry, found a box of crackers, and set it beside the last sandwich without a word, an offering for whoever was still hungry after. Walker reached for it.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles.
story:
Alexander had claimed the good armchair an hour before kickoff, which everyone agreed was gratuitous, since the game was still two hours away and he was just sitting there eating chips with the bowl balanced on his stomach like a small, salty planet. His grandfather claimed the couch. Karl and Marcus came through the door with a bag of store-brand soda and an argument they had apparently been having since the parking lot.

"It's not a dysphemism to call them the Bungles," Marcus was saying. "It's just accurate reporting."

"It's a mean nickname," Karl said. "You're maligning a whole city for one bad decade."

Alexander's mother called from the kitchen that if they were going to fight, they could fight about the commercials like civilized people. The room filled up: his father, his aunt, the neighbor Mr. Do with his famous seven-layer dip, which he carried in both hands like live ordnance. Outside the window the February light was already going gray, and the lamp made the whole living room smell faintly of warm dust and onion.

The game was close for a quarter, then not close, and somewhere in the third the grandfather leaned back and said, "You kids don't know anything about football. I remember the very first Super Bowl. I was there in spirit. Green Bay Packers against Kansas City, 35 to 10. I remember it like yesterday."

"Grandpa," Alexander said slowly, "you were born in 1963."

"So?"

"The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967. You were three."

"It was 1967?"

"January fifteenth. Packers won, 35 to 10, and it wasn't even in Green Bay, it was in Los Angeles. What were you doing in Los Angeles at age three?"

The grandfather chewed a chip with enormous dignity. Karl and Marcus had gone quiet the way people go quiet when someone else's family is about to produce theater. Mr. Do set down his dip.

"I remember my father watching it," the grandfather said at last. "I remember him jumping up and spilling something on the rug when the Packers scored. That's my Super Bowl memory, and I've been telling it wrong for twenty years, and nobody ever checked, because you're all too polite." He pointed the chip at Alexander. "This one checks."

Alexander had checked. He had looked it up on his phone under the table in the first quarter, partly to win, partly because he genuinely wanted to know whether the old man had been in Los Angeles as a toddler, which seemed like a family secret worth having. On the screen the fact sat there plain as a bus schedule: January 15, 1967, Packers over Chiefs, 35 to 10, Los Angeles. He felt the specific pleasure of a fact confirmed, and then, immediately after it, a smaller, stranger feeling. His grandfather had been three years old, in a living room somewhere, while his own father jumped up and spilled a drink. Now the grandfather was in this living room, jumping up for much less, spilling nothing yet, and someday Alexander would be the one claiming to remember this afternoon, this exact game, this dip, these idiots on the couch. Would he remember it right? Would it matter if he didn't?

"It's not lying," the grandfather was saying to Marcus, who had apparently been prosecuting the case while Alexander drifted. "It's inherited memory. Like a rug stain."

"Grandpa," Alexander said, "I think you can keep the memory. Just fix the shipping label." He held up the phone. "You remember your dad watching the first Super Bowl, and the Packers beat the Chiefs 35 to 10, and that's a true thing that happened to you. You just weren't at the game."

"I never said I was at the game," the grandfather said, with the clean shamelessness of a man who absolutely had.

"You said you were there in spirit."

"My spirit was in Los Angeles. My body was on a rug."

Mr. Do laughed so hard the dip trembled, and Alexander's mother came in from the kitchen asking what she'd missed, and Marcus tried to explain and got as far as "Grandpa's spirit was in Los Angeles in 1967" before she turned around and went back to the oven. The grandfather settled deeper into the couch, satisfied, as though he had won an argument no one else had noticed starting. On the TV somebody fumbled, and the whole room made the same noise at the same time, a low communal groan that Alexander suspected he would remember, accurately or not, for a very long time.

Karl leaned over and stole a chip. "So if the Packers played the Chiefs tomorrow, who're you taking?"

"Packers, 35 to 10," the grandfather said instantly. "Some things you remember in your bones."

"Grandpa, that was fifty-eight years ago."

"And the bones don't update." He reached for the chip bowl and found Alexander's hand already guarding it. "Boy, in this house the elders eat first."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Under the US Credit CARD Act of 2009, card statements must show how long it would take to pay off the balance by making only the minimum payment.
story:
Gabrielle stood in line at the bank with her mother's card statement folded in her back pocket, where she'd been carrying it since breakfast like evidence. Her mother had gone to work and left a list: deposit the birthday checks, ask about a savings account for Gabrielle, come straight home. The line moved slowly enough that Gabrielle had time to read the statement again, all the small gray paragraphs she'd skimmed at the kitchen table. Near the bottom, in a box she'd almost missed, it said that if she made only the minimum payment, it would take eleven years to pay off the balance.

Eleven years. She would be twenty-seven. She would have finished college, maybe started a job, and the balance from one winter of repairs and groceries would still be there, growing by itself the way frost spreads across a window. She read the line a third time to be sure she wasn't inventing it, and then the teller called her forward.

"Deposit first," she said, sliding the checks under the glass, "and then I'm supposed to ask about a savings account." The teller, an older man with reading glasses pushed up into his hair, typed while she watched. He said the savings account would earn interest, a small percentage added every month. "So the bank pays me," Gabrielle said, "the same way we pay it on the card." He nodded without looking up, and something about the symmetry of it sat uneasily in her chest, two identical words pointed in opposite directions.

She took the receipt to the waiting area, where Kara was already sitting, having texted twenty minutes earlier that she was coming to open her first credit card. Kara's eighteenth-cousin logic, as Gabrielle thought of it, was that a card would mean freedom now and paying later, and later was an abstraction, a country she'd never visited. "Guess what," Kara said before Gabrielle sat down. "If I just pay the minimum every month, I can basically spend whatever I want forever."

"Read this." Gabrielle handed her the statement, her thumb under the box. Kara's face went through its changes quickly, the confidence, the squint, the small collapse. "That can't be legal," she said. "They have to tell you that? They just admit it?" Gabrielle said that apparently they did, that the statement had to show how long paying only the minimum would take, and eleven years was what it took, printed right there by the bank itself. Kara stared at the number as if it might blink.

Mr. Ndlovu, who coached debate at their school and was at the next window cashing a cheque, came over when he saw them, because he could never resist a cluster of agitated teenagers. Kara explained the situation with theatrical despair, calling it legalized theft, and Mr. Ndlovu said, mildly, "Laws like that exist so people can choose with open eyes. Whether they choose well is another matter." He wished them luck and left, and Gabrielle found herself annoyed with the evenness of it, the way he could hold both sides like a pair of scales.

"I still want one," Kara said, quieter now. "Not for, like, hedonism or whatever. My mom's car needs tires, and there's no money till spring." Gabrielle looked down at the statement in her lap, at her own new savings receipt beside it, two papers with the same bank's logo, one promising her money would grow and the other documenting money that fed on itself. She had come here thinking the card was simply a trap, and the trap was real, she still believed that, but Kara's tires were also real, and spring was a long way from November.

"You could get it," Gabrielle said slowly, "and pay more than the minimum. Even a little more. The box only says what happens if you don't." Kara turned the statement over, then back, as if the reverse side might contradict the front. "And you'd still have it for emergencies, which I guess is the point of it anyway, the point of anything with a risk." She wasn't sure she believed her own advice; she was sixteen and had never owed anyone anything, and there was a version of this where she was wrong about how easy discipline would turn out to be for someone else's life. "Okay," Kara said, standing up and smoothing the statement flat on her knee before handing it back. "But you're coming with me to read every box before I sign."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The bleachers at the community field smelled like sunscreen and burnt hot dogs, and Emma had claimed the best seat, third row, where the sun wouldn't be in her eyes during the second half. Around her sat her father, her little brother, and half the neighborhood, all of them watching the championship game between the two strongest teams in the county league. Aleena had saved a spot beside her, and Quinton had arrived late, out of breath, carrying a bag of chips he refused to share with anyone under five feet tall, which was cruel, because that described Emma's brother exactly.

The game had been close for an hour, and then, with four minutes left, it stopped being close and started being controversial. The wing sprinted down the sideline, reached for the ball, tumbled over the line, and the referee's arm went up for a try while half the crowd roared and the other half roared louder, in the other direction. Emma's father stood up. "His foot was out," he announced to the field, to the referee, to a child three rows down who had nothing to do with any of it. "Anyone with eyes saw it."

Aleena pulled out her phone. "I'll find the livestream, they loop these things forever." But the league's livestream was twenty seconds behind reality, and when it caught up, the camera had been following the wrong player entirely. The wing's foot, in or out, existed nowhere on any screen. The crowd around them grew obstreperous, in the way crowds do when they all believe different versions of the same three seconds. Two men behind Emma were arguing about whether the grass near the line had been wet, as though that settled something.

"None of you saw it," Emma said to Aleena, quietly. "You were looking at the ball."

"So were you."

"I was looking at the line judge," Emma said, and this was true, and also, she realized, useless, because the line judge had been blocked by the water cart. She had, in effect, watched the whole play without seeing the one part that mattered. Her brother was now demanding, at volume, that somebody "replay it," the way he'd seen done on television his entire life, as if the sky might simply rewind itself on request.

That was when Ms. Traoré, who lived two streets over and came to every game with a folding chair and a thermos of tea, leaned in from the row below. "You know," she said, mostly to the brother but in a voice meant for everyone, "instant replay wasn't always there. The first one on television was CBS, during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963. A director named Tony Verna devised the whole system." She sipped her tea. "Before that, if you missed it, you missed it."

The brother stared at her. "So how did people fight?"

"With their whole hearts," Ms. Traoré said, "and no evidence at all."

Emma thought about that while the teams reset for the conversion. She had grown up believing that a disputed play was a temporary condition, that the truth would arrive on a screen within seconds, that being wrong was a bug the cameras had fixed. But there was another way of thinking sitting right next to her, older and stranger: that a game was something you witnessed once, together, and argued about forever after, and that the arguing was part of it. Her father, she noticed, was already enjoying himself enormously. He didn't want the footage. He wanted the dispute.

"Here's the thing," Aleena said, watching the stream buffer on her phone. "If we had the replay, your dad would just say the angle was bad."

"He would," Emma admitted. "He'd reify the frame. Pick one frozen image and declare it the whole truth." She'd learned the word that week in English and had been waiting, with some impatience, for a chance to deploy it. Aleena made a face that meant impressive and ridiculous at once.

"Deploying vocab at a sports field," Quinton said, having overheard. "Bold phenotype." He gestured at her sun hat, her annotated program, her seat in the shade chosen for optimal viewing. "The nerdy spectator in its natural habitat."

"You're eating chips you won't share," Emma said. "Darwin would study you."

The try stood. The conversion went wide, which satisfied nobody, and the game came down to a final kick that wobbled over the crossbar by a margin so thin that the crowd immediately began disputing it, too. Aleena held up her phone: the livestream, faithful to the end, had captured a beautiful shot of the water cart.

Walking out through the gate, Emma decided she would hold both ideas at once and let them sit uneasily together, like the two teams sharing a parking lot. She thought cameras were probably good. She thought Ms. Traoré's version of the world, where you had to live with not knowing, might be more honest, though she wasn't sure, and she wasn't going to pretend to be. Her brother was still grumbling that the technology existed and the league simply refused to use it, which, Emma pointed out, was arguably the most human thing anyone had done all afternoon.

At the edge of the field Ms. Traoré was folding her chair, and Emma caught up with her. "Did people at that game in 1963 know it was the first time?"

"They found out after," Ms. Traoré said, snapping the chair shut. "Some of them thought the picture had frozen."

"I would have panicked."

"You would have thrown something," Ms. Traoré said, and handed her the thermos to carry to the car.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
The draft came back on a Tuesday, folded once, with a red circle around the last sentence of the first paragraph and a single question beside it: what are you actually arguing? Marcus read it three times on the bus and then again at his grandfather's kitchen table, where he was supposed to spend the week getting the paper into shape. His thesis was that the transcontinental railroad changed the American economy. It had seemed solid when he wrote it. Now the circle sat there like a hole in the ice.

"Ravi's coming to look at the pipes," his grandfather said, setting down two mugs, "so we're working in the study." The study smelled of pencil shavings and old paper. His grandfather had been a copy editor at a city paper for forty years and still kept a jar of blue pencils on the shelf, though Marcus had never once seen him take one down.

Marcus spread the draft out. He had eleven index cards of notes and three books from the school library, and none of it seemed to answer Ms. Mensah's question. He texted Dani, who had gotten a similar circle on her own draft, and she wrote back: "she says our thesis has to be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, not just a fact everyone already accepts." He stared at that. His sentence wasn't a claim at all, he realized; nobody sane would stand up and say the railroad had changed nothing. He was reporting, the way he'd report the time of a soccer match.

While he worked, his grandfather moved around the study doing quiet things, and Marcus barely noticed until a drawer stuck and the old man knelt to wrestle it open. Inside was a bundle of yellowed clippings tied with string. Marcus watched him lift the bundle out and hold it without untying it, the way you'd hold something you weren't sure you wanted to see.

The old man's hands were steadier than he felt. He had written one real piece in his life, an opinion column in 1968 about the paper's own coverage of a strike, and it had been killed before it ran. He had never told the boy any of this. Forty years of fixing other people's sentences, and the one argument that had been his own was still in this drawer, typed on the back of galley proofs. He set the bundle on the desk between them. "Before you rewrite," he said, "read something."

Marcus untied the string. The column argued that the paper had covered the strike as a disruption to commuters rather than as a dispute between men and management, and that the choice of frame was itself a position. It was sharp and it was angry and it took a side that a reasonable reader could have torn into. Two pages later, clipped to the rejection memo, was an editor's note: well made, but not for us. His grandfather said nothing while Marcus read, only drank his coffee, though Marcus caught him watching over the rim of the mug.

Here was what Marcus had been missing, though it took him another hour of drafting to say it plainly. He had been beguiled by the safety of facts, by the way a sentence nobody could fight with also meant a sentence nobody could fight for. He tried a new thesis: that the railroad's economic gains were paid for unequally, concentrated in financiers and freight interests while laborers and Indigenous communities along the route absorbed the costs. Dani would dispute it. Ravi, if he ever emerged from under the sink, might dispute it. That was the point. On a fresh card he wrote the word arguable and underlined it twice, then flipped the card over and wrote uncertainty: how much weight do the land grant records carry, and is that a question I can actually settle in eight pages? He left the question there, honest, unresolved.

The last paragraph of the old column described the montane country the strike's miners had come from, high valleys where a man could see weather coming for an hour before it arrived, and Marcus copied the phrase onto his card about sources, because the clipping his grandfather had saved beside it, a letter to the editor from a miner's widow, was the kind of source no encyclopedia would ever hand you. He asked if he could use it. "It's yours if you footnote it properly," his grandfather said, and pulled a blue pencil from the jar at last, circling the word Bibliography at the bottom of Marcus's outline. "This goes on its own page. Alphabetical. You'll thank me when you're not doing it at midnight."

By evening Marcus had a new first paragraph, an argument a person could push back against, and a stack of index cards arranged like evidence at a trial. He read the opening aloud at the kitchen table while his grandfather made sandwiches. "The transcontinental railroad's benefits were real but radically uneven," Marcus read, "and the records of who paid for them have not been evenly kept." The old man set down the bread knife, took the page, and read it to himself, his lips barely moving, the way he had read ten thousand pages before it. Then he handed it back and said, "Now you're writing something."

Ravi called from the basement that the pipes were fixed, and the water ran clean in the kitchen sink.
